title: Longest Subarray of 1's After Deleting One Element
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every subarray's zero count directly versus a variable-size sliding window that allows at most one zero.

sections.title: Longest Subarray of 1's After Deleting One Element

content.title: Longest Subarray of 1's After Deleting One Element

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a binary array nums, delete exactly one element from it, and return the size of the longest contiguous subarray containing only 1s in the result. If no such subarray exists after the deletion, return 0.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums, a binary array"],["Output","The length of the longest run of 1s achievable after deleting exactly one element"],["Goal","Find the best deletion without literally trying every possible one"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 100000; nums[i] is 0 or 1"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A window is allowed at most one \"bad\" element (a 0), since it will be deleted","A variable-size sliding window allowing at most one zero"],["Exactly one element must always be deleted, even if the window is already all 1s","The answer is always window length minus 1, never the raw window length"]]}

blocks.text: Find a contiguous window of nums that contains at most one 0. Deleting that one 0 (or, if the window is already all 1s, deleting any one of its 1s, since exactly one deletion is required) leaves a run of all 1s whose length is the window's length minus 1. Maximize that value over every possible window.

blocks.title: Analogy: Removing One Weak Link From the Longest Possible Chain
blocks.text: Picture a chain of links, some strong (1) and some weak (0), and being required to remove exactly one link. The best result comes from finding the longest stretch of chain containing at most one weak link, removing that single weak link (or any link, if the stretch is already all strong), and keeping the rest.

blocks.caption: A window with at most one zero; deleting it leaves window length minus 1 ones

blocks.text: Deleting the single 0 leaves [1,1,1], a run of length 3.
Deleting the 0 at index 4 leaves the subarray [1,1,1,_,1,1] effectively joining into a run of length 5 around it.
Edge case: nums = [1,1,1] (no zeros at all)
Even though the whole array is already 1s, exactly one element must still be deleted, leaving a run of length 2, not 3.
Before checking every possible subarray directly, notice this is exactly a "longest window with at most one bad element" problem, with one extra twist at the end.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Any window containing at most one 0 can be turned into an all-1s run by deleting that one 0.

Observation 2: If a window contains zero 0s already, exactly one deletion is still required by the problem, so one of its 1s must go, leaving window length minus 1.

Observation 3: A window with more than one 0 cannot be fixed with only one deletion, so any valid window must expand while keeping its zero count at 1 or fewer.

Observation 4: A classic two-pointer sliding window, expanding the right edge and shrinking the left edge whenever the zero count exceeds 1, finds the longest such window in one pass.
This leads to a variable-size sliding window allowing at most one zero, with the final answer always being the best window length found, minus 1, to account for the mandatory single deletion.
Check every possible subarray directly, and among those containing at most one 0, track the maximum length minus 1.

items: For every starting index i and ending index j (i at most j), count the zeros in nums[i..j] directly.
If that count is 0 or 1, the subarray can become all 1s after one deletion, so consider its length minus 1.
Track the maximum such value across every subarray.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every subarray directly for its zero count

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every starting index restarts its own zero count and extends j outward, re-deriving the zero count for every ending position from that start.
The moment the zero count exceeds 1 for a given start, no larger j from that same start needs checking, but every start is still tried independently.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), every pair of start and end indices is examined.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: restarting the zero count from every possible starting index repeats work that a single expanding-and-shrinking window could share across all starting points.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why restarting from every index is wasteful: as the window's right edge grows, only the left edge needs to move forward when the zero count becomes too large, it never needs to jump backward.

What is the shrinking rule: whenever the window holds more than one zero, move the left edge forward, decrementing the zero count whenever the element leaving the window was itself a zero, until the count is back to at most 1.

The core idea: expand the right edge one step at a time, shrink the left edge only when needed to maintain at most one zero, and track window length minus 1 at every step.

Expand a right pointer across the array, incrementing a zero counter whenever a 0 is included. Whenever that counter exceeds 1, advance a left pointer, decrementing the counter whenever the element leaving is a 0, until the counter is back to at most 1. At every step, record the current window length minus 1 as a candidate answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["right","Zero count","Action","Best so far (length minus 1)"],"rows":[["0 (value 0)","1","window is [0]","0"],["1..3 (values 1,1,1)","1","window grows to [0,1,1,1]","3"],["4 (value 0)","2","shrink left past the first 0","3 (window now [1,1,1,0])"],["5..6 (values 1,1)","1","window grows to [1,1,1,0,1,1]","5"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: expand right, shrink left only when the zero count exceeds one

blocks.text: Both the left and right pointers only ever move forward, never backward, so the window is adjusted in amortized O(1) per step. Since the window always holds at most one zero by the time its length is recorded, that single zero (or a single 1, if the window has none) accounts for exactly the one mandatory deletion, making window length minus 1 the correct candidate at every step.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since both pointers together traverse the array at most twice.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: This is the classic "longest subarray with at most one bad element" sliding window, with one small twist: the answer is always window length minus 1, since exactly one deletion is mandatory even when the window is already all 1s.

items: Forgetting to subtract 1 from the window length, since a deletion is always mandatory, even for an all-1s window.
Shrinking the window as soon as any zero is seen, instead of only when the zero count exceeds 1.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["nums is all 1s","The answer is nums.length minus 1, since one 1 must still be deleted."],["nums is all 0s","The answer is 0, no run of 1s survives."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating the "minus 1 for the mandatory deletion" rule up front, and confirming it applies even to an all-1s window, heads off the most common bug in this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "what if the array has no zeros at all", think: exactly one deletion is still required, so the answer is window length minus 1, not the raw length.

Why do both pointers only ever need to move forward, never backward, across the whole pass?
The "longest subarray with at most k bad elements" family of sliding window problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized sliding window runs in O(n) time. Both use O(1) space.

items: Pattern: variable-size sliding window allowing at most one "bad" element (a zero).
Core Idea: expand the window while at most one zero is present, shrink from the left only when a second zero appears, and the answer is always window length minus 1.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized sliding window.
Most Important Observation: exactly one deletion is mandatory, so the answer is never the raw window length, always length minus 1.
Interview Difficulty: a standard sliding window, made slightly trickier by the mandatory-deletion edge case.
One line memory trick: longest window with at most one zero, minus one for the deletion you must always make.
